specification.problem: Reconstruct the mathematical content of Shor's factoring algorithm (SFA) with the quantum order finding algorithm (QOFA) as its subroutine, together with the classical post-processing rule by which an odd order r can still yield the factors of N = p_1 p_2 when the chosen coprime a is a perfect square a = b^2, as described in the abstract.
specification.reconstruction_scope: One run of the QOFA (standard phase-estimation order finding) for the smallest explicit instance in which an odd order with a square coprime yields the factors: N = 21, a = 4 = 2^2 (so b = 2), whose order is r = 3 (odd). The scope covers: definition of the order, the controlled-modular-multiplication unitary and its eigenphases, the phase-estimation measurement and continued-fraction recovery of r, the standard even-order factor extraction, and the inferred odd-order square-coprime extraction rule via b^r. Outside scope: the paper's second technique ('looking out for new order finding relations in the case of failure'), its quantitative analysis of the success-probability improvement, the claimed efficiency equivalence with avoiding square coprimes, and any specific circuit decomposition of modular multiplication.

symbols.meaning: Composite number to be factored, N = p_1 p_2
symbols.domain: odd composite positive integer; instance N = 21

symbols.meaning: Randomly chosen base coprime to N (here chosen as a square a = b^2 mod N)
symbols.domain: integer, 1 < a < N, gcd(a,N) = 1; instance a = 4

symbols.meaning: Square root of the coprime, a \equiv b^2 \pmod N, assumed known
symbols.domain: integer, 1 < b < N, gcd(b,N) = 1; instance b = 2

symbols.meaning: Multiplicative order of a modulo N
Number of qubits in the work register, n = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil
Number of qubits in the control (phase) register
Modular multiplication-by-a unitary on the work register
Index of the U_a eigenstate selected by the measurement
Integer measurement outcome of the control register
Computational basis state encoding integer x with qubit j holding bit x_j, x = \sum_j x_j 2^j (qubit 0 is least significant)

equations.label: Definition of the order
equations.description: The order r is the smallest positive integer with a^r mod N = 1; it is the quantity computed by the QOFA.
equations.abstract_quote: calculates the order – the smallest integer, $r$, satisfying $a^{r}\mod N=1$, where $a$ is a randomly chosen integer coprime to $N$

equations.label: Even-order factor extraction
equations.latex: r \text{ even},\; a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N \;\Rightarrow\; p_1 = \gcd\!\left(a^{r/2}-1,\,N\right),\quad p_2 = \gcd\!\left(a^{r/2}+1,\,N\right)
equations.description: Standard classical post-processing of Shor's algorithm: for even r with a^{r/2} not congruent to -1, the two gcds give the nontrivial factors. The abstract states this holds with probability at least 1/2 over the random choice of a.
equations.abstract_quote: the factors are given by $p_{1}=\gcd(a^{\frac{r}{2}}-1,N)$ and $p_{2}=\gcd(a^{\frac{r}{2}}+1,N)$
equations.justification: Stated in the abstract; the explicit side-condition a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 (mod N) is added from standard background to make the relation exact.
assumptions: The condition a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N is the standard requirement for the gcds to be nontrivial; the abstract folds this into the 'probability not less than 1/2' statement.

equations.label: Modular multiplication unitary and its eigenphases
equations.latex: U_a|y\rangle = \begin{cases}|a y \bmod N\rangle & 0 \le y < N\\ |y\rangle & N \le y < 2^n\end{cases}, \qquad U_a|u_s\rangle = e^{2\pi i s/r}|u_s\rangle,\quad |u_s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=0}^{r-1} e^{-2\pi i s k/r}|a^k \bmod N\rangle,\quad |1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}|u_s\rangle
equations.description: The QOFA is phase estimation of U_a; its eigenvalues encode s/r, and the easily prepared state |1> is a uniform superposition of the eigenstates.
equations.justification: Standard formulation of order finding as phase estimation; the abstract only names the QOFA.
assumptions: The work register has n = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil qubits and U_a acts as identity on basis states y \ge N.

equations.label: Phase estimation state and order recovery
equations.latex: \frac{1}{2^{t/2}}\sum_{x=0}^{2^t-1}|x\rangle|a^{x} \bmod N\rangle \xrightarrow{\mathrm{QFT}^{-1}_{t}} \;\text{measure } m,\qquad \left|\frac{m}{2^t} - \frac{s}{r}\right| \le \frac{1}{2^{t+1}} \text{ with probability } \ge \frac{4}{\pi^2},\qquad 2^t \ge 2N^2 \Rightarrow \frac{s}{r} \text{ is the unique convergent of } \frac{m}{2^t} \text{ with denominator } < N
equations.description: After controlled modular exponentiation and inverse QFT on the control register, the outcome m approximates 2^t s/r; continued fractions recover a candidate r (the denominator of the convergent, exact only when gcd(s,r)=1).
equations.justification: Standard analysis of Shor's order finding; the approximation is not exact equality, and the recovered denominator may be a divisor of r when gcd(s,r) > 1, which is checked classically via a^{r'} mod N.
assumptions: Control register size t with 2^t \ge 2N^2 (t = 2n suffices up to rounding; t = 10 chosen for N = 21).
Controlled-U_a^{2^j} is applied with control qubit j of the control register.

equations.label: Odd-order factor extraction for a square coprime
equations.latex: a \equiv b^2 \pmod N,\; r \text{ odd} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2r} \equiv 1 \pmod N;\qquad b^{r} \not\equiv \pm 1 \pmod N \;\Rightarrow\; p_1 = \gcd\!\left(b^{r}-1,\,N\right),\; p_2 = \gcd\!\left(b^{r}+1,\,N\right)
equations.description: If the coprime is a known square a = b^2, an odd order r of a implies (b^r)^2 ≡ 1 mod N, so b^r is a square root of unity; whenever it is a nontrivial square root, the gcds give the factors. This is the mechanism by which odd orders can lead to factors.
equations.abstract_quote: the factors can sometimes be found from odd orders if the coprime is square
equations.justification: The abstract asserts that odd orders can yield factors when the coprime is square; the stated relation is the natural inference (b^r plays the role of a^{r/2}), with the exceptional case b^r \equiv \pm 1 explaining the word 'sometimes'. The paper's exact formulation is not available.
assumptions: b with a \equiv b^2 \pmod N is known to the experimenter (e.g., a is chosen as b^2).
The abstract does not state the side-condition b^r \not\equiv \pm 1; it is supplied here as the standard requirement for nontrivial gcds.

equations.label: Tiny explicit instance
equations.description: Worked instance: the order of the square coprime a = 4 modulo 21 is odd (r = 3), eq_2 is inapplicable, but eq_5 with b = 2 recovers the factors 3 and 7. Expected QPE outcomes with t = 10 cluster near m \approx 1024 s/3 \in \{0, 341.33, 682.67\}.
equations.justification: Chosen as the smallest explicit instance exhibiting an odd order with a square coprime that leads to the factors; not taken from the abstract.
assumptions: Instance choice N = 21, a = 4, b = 2 is the reconstructor's choice, not from the paper.

registers.name: control (phase) register
registers.role: Holds the superposition over exponents x and, after inverse QFT, the measured approximation m of 2^t s/r; qubit j (0 = least significant) controls U_a^{2^j}.

registers.name: work register
registers.role: Holds integers modulo N in binary (qubit 0 least significant); initialized to |1> and acted on by controlled modular multiplications by a^{2^j} mod N.

specification.initial_state: |0\rangle^{\otimes t} \otimes |1\rangle, i.e. control register all zeros and work register encoding the integer 1 (= uniform superposition of U_a eigenstates |u_s>, eq_3).

steps.description: Classically choose b coprime to N and set a = b^2 mod N (here b = 2, a = 4, N = 21); verify gcd(a,N) = 1 (if gcd > 1 a factor is found directly).
Apply Hadamard gates to all t control qubits to prepare (1/2^{t/2}) \sum_x |x\rangle|1\rangle.
For j = 0,...,t-1 apply controlled-U_{a^{2^j} mod N} with control qubit j of the control register, producing (1/2^{t/2}) \sum_x |x\rangle |a^x mod N\rangle.
Apply the inverse quantum Fourier transform on the control register.
Measure the control register to obtain m; run the continued-fraction expansion of m/2^t to obtain a candidate denominator r'; verify a^{r'} ≡ 1 mod N (otherwise try small multiples of r' or repeat).

Classical post-processing: if r is even and a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1, output gcd(a^{r/2} ± 1, N). If r is odd and a = b^2 with known b, compute b^r mod N; if b^r \not\equiv ±1 output gcd(b^r ± 1, N) (for the instance: 7 and 3). Otherwise relaunch with a different a.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of all t control-register qubits, read as the integer m = \sum_j m_j 2^j; the work register is not measured (or measured and discarded).
specification.classical_postprocessing: Continued-fraction expansion of m/2^t to recover s/r in lowest terms (denominator is r or a divisor thereof; verify with a^{r} mod N). Then apply eq_2 for even r, or the odd-order square-coprime rule eq_5 for odd r when a = b^2 with b known; both rules use only gcd computations. Failure cases (a^{r/2} ≡ -1 or b^r ≡ ±1) lead to relaunching the QOFA with a new a.
assumptions: No experiment scope was supplied; the smallest useful construction (one QOFA run for N = 21, a = 4 = 2^2, r = 3) was chosen by the reconstructor.
Control register size t = 10 (2^t ≥ 2N^2 = 882) is a standard choice, not from the abstract.
The square root b of the coprime a is known (a is chosen as b^2), which is what makes the odd-order rule eq_5 usable.
Little-endian integer encoding (qubit 0 least significant) in both registers.
The side-conditions a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 and b^r \not\equiv ±1 (mod N) are supplied from standard number theory; the abstract only says the odd-order approach works 'sometimes'.
missing_information: The paper's second technique, 'looking out for new order finding relations in the case of failure', is not described mathematically in the abstract and could not be reconstructed.
The quantitative size of the success-probability improvement from using odd orders is not given.
The precise argument for the claimed efficiency equivalence between the new techniques and 'avoiding square coprimes and disregarding odd orders' is not available.
Whether the paper's odd-order rule requires b to be known in advance, or recovers it otherwise, is not stated.
No circuit-level decomposition of controlled modular multiplication by a^{2^j} mod N is provided; this is left to the circuit-generation stage.
